tagline: Desert plants, mining towns and a tunnel climbing through solid rock.
intro: US 60 crosses four plant and animal communities on the Gila-Pinal Scenic Road, from Sonoran Desert to ponderosa pine. The Forest Service describes this scenic byway as 35 paved miles between Florence Junction and Miami, with hills and inclines, Picketpost Mountain and waterside habitats along Arnett and Pinto creeks. East of Superior, the road climbs through the 1,217-foot Queen Creek Tunnel at a six percent grade.

The Superior-to-Miami road was constructed in 1920–22. The smaller Claypool Tunnel followed in 1926, but the crossing continued to change. An Arizona Highway Department improvement program began in 1937 and culminated in the Queen Creek Tunnel’s completion in 1952. Fisher Contracting Company cut the replacement through solid rock in Queen Creek gorge. At the dedication, the drill rig served as a platform for officials and a brass band.

Traveling east, Boyce Thompson Arboretum sits beneath Picketpost Mountain, three miles west of Superior. Superior’s mines first produced silver, then copper. Beyond town come the tunnel and Top-of-the-World, on the divide between Superior and Miami at 4,600 feet. The drive ends in Miami, a copper town on the northeastern slope of the Pinal Mountains. Its Bullion Plaza Museum presents the area’s cultural, mining and ranching history.

moments.title: Boyce Thompson Arboretum
moments.text: A copper fortune helped build this collection of desert plants. Mining engineer William Boyce Thompson founded the arboretum in 1924 as a research facility; it opened to the public in 1929. Along Queen Creek beneath Picketpost Mountain, more than 2,600 species of arid-land plants grow in gardens that include cacti, aloes and eucalyptus. A looping primary trail extends 1.5 miles through exhibits and natural areas. Among the eucalyptus is Mr. Big, one of the largest red gum eucalyptus trees in the United States. The garden connects Thompson’s mining career with his separate investment in plant research.
moments.notice: The eucalyptus grove includes Mr. Big, one of the largest red gum eucalyptus trees in the United States.

moments.title: Queen Creek Tunnel
moments.text: The climb continues inside Queen Creek Tunnel: its roadbed rises at six percent. Completed in 1952, the 1,217-foot passage replaced the smaller Claypool Tunnel of 1926. Cutting through rock solved one problem, but lighting created another. The original system gave motorists inadequate depth perception on the grade. Fluorescent lights improved visibility in the 1960s, and an LED system followed in 2016. That system adjusts to the light and weather outside. The tunnel’s history is a sequence of changes to the same crossing, from the size of the opening to the way drivers see their passage through it.

moments.title: Top-of-the-World
moments.text: Top-of-the-World occupies the divide between Superior and Miami at 4,600 feet, with US 60 running through the community. The name has traveled. Mason’s Valley is also called Pinal Ranch and Top-of-the-World, but the latter name came from a camping and recreation facility established in 1922 on an old US 60 alignment, about two miles west. The valley takes its own name from Charles G. Mason, a prospector involved in developing the Silver King Mine north of Superior. Highway travel and mining both appear in the names attached to this mountain crossing.
